title: Randomized product formulas beyond optimal deterministic scaling
abstract: Product formulas, also known as Trotter formulas, are among the most widely used and practical methods for simulating quantum systems on quantum computers. Here we introduce two new classes of randomized product formulas for simulating Hamiltonians with separated energy scales, $H=A+αB$, where $α$ is small. In the standard access model, where one can implement exponentials of $A$ and $B$ separately, our randomized formulas achieve $\mathcal O(α^2)$ error scaling at the cost of only doubling the gate depth of the corresponding deterministic formula. We further prove an $Ω(α)$ lower bound for deterministic product formulas. In a stronger access model, allowing exponentials of $A+αB_\ell$ for $B = \sum_{\ell}B_\ell$, our randomized formula, based on Trotter Heuristic Resource Improved Formulas for Time-dynamics (THRIFT)~[J. L. Bosse et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2673 (2025)], achieves $\mathcal O(α^3)$ error scaling with only constant-factor expected gate overhead. We also establish an $Ω(α^2)$ lower bound for deterministic product formulas in this access model. Numerical simulations confirm gate-count reductions for simulating physically motivated systems.
summary: The paper introduces novel randomized product formulas to simulate quantum dynamics governed by $H = A + \alpha B$. By averaging over random shifts, these methods achieve significantly better error scaling (e.g., $O(\alpha^3)$) than deterministic protocols. This breakthrough is vital for efficiently simulating weakly coupled quantum systems on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing randomized product formulas that overcome fundamental error scaling limitations inherent in deterministic methods for simulating quantum time evolution.
main_result: Randomized formulas achieve superior error scaling, reaching $O(\alpha^3)$ or better, while maintaining a low expected gate overhead compared to the $\Omega(\alpha)$ or $\Omega(\alpha^2)$ lower bounds proven for deterministic counterparts.
method: The authors introduce randomized product formulas by averaging over random shifts in the Trotter steps, which allows error terms that persist deterministically to cancel out through expectation values.
model_or_system: The simulation targets quantum systems governed by a Hamiltonian $H = A + \alpha B$, where $\alpha$ is small. The analysis considers two access models: one allowing separate exponentials of $A$ and $B$, and a stronger model allowing implementation of $e^{-is(A+\alpha B_\ell)}$ for components $B_\ell$.
key_observables: Error scaling (measured by the diamond norm, $\|\cdot\|_\diamond$), expected gate count ($	ext{E}_\omega[G]$), and comparison against lower bounds.
important_parameters: The small coupling strength $\alpha$, the number of Trotter steps ($r$), and the order of approximation ($2k$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on $\alpha \ll 1$ and uses techniques like Dyson series expansions, telescoping identities, and bounding mixed derivatives.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics comparing deterministic vs. randomized formulas (Fig. 1), detail the dyadic sampling strategy for THRIFT (Fig. 2), and benchmark gate counts/error scaling for physical models (Figs. 3 & 4).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes two access models, deriving improved error bounds using randomization techniques based on Trotter-Heuristic Resource Improved Formulas (THRIFT) and establishing corresponding lower bounds that prove the necessity of randomization.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the efficiency bottleneck in quantum simulation algorithms by providing provably superior scaling for time evolution approximations when interactions are weak, which is crucial for simulating many physical systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

(a) The de- terministic 1st-order formula, (e−iδtαBe−iδtA)r. (b) One instance of the 1st-order randomized formula, Eq. (3). (c) One instance of the 2nd-order randomized formula, Eq. (9), obtained by symmetrizing (b); higher-order for- mulas are recursively constructed from this via Eq. (10).
FIG. 2: Dyadic sampling for randomized THRIFT. Sam- pled rectangles in the time-ordering triangle specify the local corrections in Eq. (22).

FIG. 4: Gate-count advantage of randomized first-order THRIFT for simulating the dynamics of the 8-qubit random-field Heisenberg chain at t = 9/E0, across inter- action strengths α and target errors ϵ. The color shows the ratio of the smaller median gate count of determin- istic first- and second-order THRIFT to the median ex- pected gate count of randomized first-order THRIFT. For each method, the median is taken over ten independent field realizations of the minimum gate count required to achieve the target error. In the red region, randomized first-order THRIFT requires fewer gates than either first- or second-order deterministic THRIFT.

FIG. 3: Minimum number of elementary exponentials (gates) required to simulate the dynamics of the 9-qubit transverse-field Ising model at t = 9/E0, comparing stan- dard deterministic product formulas with our random- ized formulas as a function of α. Our approach requires fewer gates for small α, while deterministic formulas per- form better as α increases since our method uses twice as many gates.
